paragraphs.text: Heaven rejoices when stars rise among the stars, and harbors when small ships gleam among the great ships, and when clouds move up and down among the clouds and sprinkle and scatter sweet dew. The church also rejoices when congregations hasten after congregations and feasts press upon feasts in the holy places. They do not change their strength according to the places, but renew their affection as the places change: from blessing to blessing, from church to church. Indeed, we ought rather to say, in the apostle’s words, “from faith to faith” and “from glory to glory.” And the prophetic word is fulfilled: “They shall go from strength to strength.” Yesterday the royal crown of the apostles made us radiant, and today the crown of the martyrs enlightens us. The church receives both the royal crown and the crown of victory, and in her the prophet’s word is fulfilled: “The church is a crown of beauty in the Lord’s hand and a royal crown in the hand of God.” But let the labors of these martyrs crown our bosoms, and the light of the lamps crown the walls of this temple, as a rampart and a bulwark. A twofold bulwark has been placed around us by the Trinity, for nothing in heaven or on earth is enlightened without the Holy Trinity. These new things imitate the original model, for the work that God does in secret these lamps also do openly. For this illumination has surrounded us like a bulwark, and he promises: “I shall be a wall of fire around my people.”

Truly the earth has been filled with the knowledge of the Lord, like abundant waters covering the seas. And even now, through the holy congregations, the prophet’s hidden saying is fulfilled: “The earth is the Lord’s, with all that fills it.” The prophets proclaimed this, but they did not speak these words with reference to the present established state of things. Who does not know that the earth is the Lord’s, with all that fills it? Or who would be uncertain whether another lord has a share in creation? For all of us, believers and unbelievers alike, plainly know through long-established custom that everything belongs to God. But the prophets spoke this not with reference to the present established state of things, but to the former error, when idolatry [?] the earth, when people grew fervent toward images, when God was not recognized and those who were not gods received worship.

When, as the apostle says, “They worshiped created things and not the Creator,” the holy prophets saw the earth as though driven into exile by some tyrant, and cried out to those who had gone astray: “The earth is the Lord’s, with all that fills it. Why do you wander astray? [?] do you reckon the regions of the earth as belonging to various gods?” For the places were called by the names of the demons. Just as a rebel invades and forcibly takes another’s kingdom for himself, so the demons entered the world and seized its various regions for themselves. Some were called gods of the Lycians, some of the people of Attica, others of the [?], and others of the Achaeans. Each had been assigned its own region, and the places were named according to the designation of the gods to whom they were dedicated. For example, the Athenians were named after the god whom they worshiped, and those of Heliopolis according to their own gods, and each people according to its own gods. And, so that I do not prolong the account by setting everything out in sequence, the places too were named after the gods.

And so that the preceding account does not mislead you, pay attention to the writings that agree with it. The people of old believed that each of the gods had been allotted a single region of the earth, and that God held the region of Judea. For the Assyrian himself said, when they came against the land of the Palestinians, “Did their gods save their respective lands, that the God of Israel should save you?” The people of old supposed that the Lord of all was one of the imagined gods; and just as each of the falsely named gods received his own land, so too, they supposed, God possesses the land of the Palestinians as his own. As the other barbarian also said, “He has authority only over the mountains of the Palestinians.” And so, to those who were in error, who divided the earth away from a single lordship and reckoned the regions under heaven to be under many lordships, they [?]: “The earth and all that fills it belong to the Lord.” Then, as though required to make clear how the whole earth belongs to the Lord, he brings forward the evidence of creation, to establish the bounds of his lordship: “He himself,” he says, “laid its foundations upon the sea and established it upon the rivers.”

From then on, the whole earth was filled with the glory of Christ, and the whole earth became full of the knowledge of the Lord, as the prophet Isaiah says: “Like the abundant waters that cover the seas.” What nature does not admit as a rule, the laws of faith establish. You know, brothers, that many rivers from every region under heaven flow into the seas, and they have not covered them. Rather, they themselves were covered and did not cover them. But the new proclamation promises a new kind of power. “The knowledge of God,” he says, “will fill the earth like the abundant waters that cover the seas.” What cannot happen by nature, he affirms concerning this knowledge. Just as a sea cannot be covered by waters from elsewhere, so the earth cannot be filled with knowledge according to the ordinary state of things. But look: the word spread and filled every corner of the earth, and the teaching of the gospel covered the seas. What sea? The one in which people were tossed about as in the depths. The word of God went forth and filled every corner under heaven, and what Daniel said was fulfilled: “The stone that was cut from the mountain without hands became a great mountain, and the whole earth was filled by it.” Sometimes he compares it to water, which covers everything under heaven; for the teaching advanced in its course, and the word fills the ends of the earth. And sometimes he compares it to a mountain, because of the height of the teaching, because its discourse about God reaches heaven. “In the last days,” he says, “the mountain of the Lord will be manifest, and the house [?] above the mountain peaks.” What house? The church. For it is not built upon mountains, but stands established in the height of its discourse about God. The church is the house of God, as Paul writes to Timothy: “So that you may know,” he says, “how you ought to conduct yourself in the house of God, which is the church.” And why upon the mountains? The Savior says, “A city standing upon a mountain cannot be hidden.”

It became the stone that was cut without hands, because Christ was born without a man. The stone was cut without hands, because Christ was born without marital intercourse; and the stone became a great mountain and filled everything under heaven. But lest anyone consider these words a forced interpretation and say, “What connection does the stone have with establishing birth in the flesh?” it is necessary to make clear that human offspring too are called stones cut from a rock. And from this it will be established that being cut means being born. The prophet Isaiah says to the people, “Look to the solid rock from which you were cut.” And to explain the rock, he adds next: “Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah, who bore you.” Do you see that he calls human births stones cut from the rock?

And why does he speak of the birth of the people as coming from a rock? Because Sarah was barren, and a rock is barren and bears no fruit. He calls her a rock, barren by nature but fruitful through grace. “Look,” he says, “to the rock from which you were cut.” Just as the stones cut from the rock there indicate the birth of the people, so here the stone cut out without hands signifies Christ’s birth in the flesh. And see how carefully he speaks. Since rocks often break off and fall from mountains without hands, he did not say that it broke off or split, but that it was cut out. For the birth according to the divine dispensation was to be brought forth, he says: “The stone was cut out without hands.” For he was not born according to the laws of nature, but through a new kind of [?]. Without experience of marriage, the flower blossomed from a virgin womb, and it became a great mountain and filled the earth. If the events did not agree with the words, then this defense is in vain, and we are trying to force the truth by falsehood. But if the events appeared before the words and cry out, and the whole earth has become filled with the knowledge of Christ, if we are ungrateful for the benefits of these deeds, we too will hear from the Lord: “Even if you remain silent, these stones will cry out.” A stone was cut out without hands and became a great mountain. And all peoples come to this mountain and say: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob.”

And pay close attention to how he first presents the conversion of the Gentiles and then the calling of the Jews. For those from among the Gentiles believe in Christ first, and after them, those from among the Jews. Many nations will follow and say: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, and he will tell us his ways, and we will follow him.” And what does he add next? “For the law,” he says, “will go out from Zion.” See how he presents the law of the second covenant, for the first law came not from Zion but from Mount Sinai. “The law,” he says, “will go out from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem, and he will judge among the nations”—and the rest of what follows, one by one. When he has foretold the conversion of the Gentiles, the prophetic Spirit then appeals to the Jews and says: “And now, house of Jacob, come, let us walk in the light of the Lord.” Do you see? First the Gentiles believe, and then the Jewish people are called.

You have the example of Joseph. The types of the Savior were fulfilled beforehand: Joseph first ruled in Egypt, and afterward over his ungrateful brothers. First he ruled over the Egyptians, who were foreigners, and afterward over his brothers, who were of his own people. And see the wonder: is not what David said fulfilled entirely in Christ? “He established it,” he says, “as a testimony in Joseph,” instead of saying that he established in Joseph a prophecy that would bear witness. If he had stayed and remained with his father Jacob, Egypt would not have received the one who provided for it. Pay close attention. If Joseph had remained there, cherished by his father, Egypt would not have received its caretaker and the one who devised a remedy for the famine. Joseph was sent to visit his brothers and the flocks; the Only Begotten was sent into the world to seek the lost sheep of the house of Israel. Dreams adorned Joseph, and miracles glorified Christ. “I saw that my brothers and I were reaping, and their sheaves bowed down to my sheaf.” For the bowing down was to happen because of the danger of famine, and God showed beforehand, through the sheaf of grain, the outcome of the events that were to come. First the sheaves bowed down to him, for his brothers were the first to bow down to him. First, the famine brought them down to Egypt, and on the second occasion they recognized their brother. The first time they stood trembling before him as before a ruler, and on the second occasion they recognized him and were honored. They recognized him and were glorified as the brothers of the glorified Joseph.

Joseph’s brothers hated him because of his dreams, and they did not know that they were hating not him, but the one who showed him the dreams. Was it by his own choice that he saw the dream? Therefore, whoever fought against the dreamer was fighting against God. But see how wickedness blinds people. Why would you fight against this dreamer? Will those dreams turn out to be true, or will they prove false? If they prove true, by what schemes could you set aside the truth? And if they prove false, why would you be jealous of this raving dreamer of the night? Joseph went to visit his brothers, to show them an act of love. But they repaid his kindness with the insult of ingratitude. He spoke words of peace to them, but they banded together to fight against him, so that the words of the Giver of Life might be fulfilled: “They hated me without cause.” See the wonders: “The dreamer is coming,” they say. The vision of the dream terrified them—or rather, not the vision, but the fear that these things would come to pass. They planned the holy man’s death, but God made their wickedness into an instrument of providence. For it is God’s work not only to bestow gifts from himself, but also to turn our wickedness to good use. They wanted to kill their brother. Reuben offered good advice: “Let us not kill him, for he is our brother and our own flesh. Instead, let us throw him into one of the pits somewhere.” And he had it in mind to find a way to save him. But [?] was carrying out the work of providence. Joseph was not killed, but went down alive into the pit, for he was a figure of the Living One, who descended alive into hell. Joseph went down into the pit, and the pit was empty of water. It was a likeness of the tomb of the Giver of Life, which was empty of the dead.

Joseph was thrown into the pit. Judah, taking pity on his brother, put forward a good proposal: not to kill him in the pit. “What benefit would there be if we killed him? Come, let us sell him.” Judah spared his brother out of concern for him, but the all-knowing God was carrying out the work of providence. It was fitting that Joseph should then be sold through Judah, for the Giver of Life was also sold through Judas the betrayer. The Ishmaelites took him and brought him to Egypt. By what means? By camel. And what were the camels carrying? Resin, [?], and incense. It was indeed fitting that the vessel of poured-out oil should be sent along with incense. One can understand from the narrative itself how wickedness unwillingly praises the one being sold, so that they might obtain a higher price. The Ishmaelites asked, “Is this young man good?” They were forced to comply, for they saw the silver in hand. “He is freeborn,” they say, “and of noble birth. He does not know how to steal; he cannot swear falsely.” Willingly, though against its will, wickedness exposed its own falsehood.

Joseph went down to Egypt, for the Giver of Life was also to go to Egypt. Joseph was sold to foreigners. Christ was handed over to the Gentiles: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over into the hands of the Gentiles.” Joseph was in the hands of the Ishmaelites, and Jesus in the hands of the Gentiles. Joseph went down to Egypt, and at first he suffered hardship. For Jesus also was not accepted by the Gentiles at first, and afterward they bowed down to the one whom they had persecuted and insulted. And he faithfully depicted the foreshadowing in Joseph’s suffering from the sexual immorality of [?]: the woman seized Joseph’s clothing, just as death seized the body of the Giver of Life. Joseph stripped off his clothing and threw it beside the wanton woman, just as the Giver of Life, when he rose, left his clothing in the tomb. Joseph entered prison, for Christ too was to enter the tomb. Joseph was ruler over the prisoners, for Christ too is king of the living and the dead.

And see the nobility of his spirit: outwardly he was in prison and in chains; the free man was in servitude; the one who would be honored with kingship was in prison. He never wavered like someone weak in faith. He did not say, “Where are the dreams? Where are the false visions?” He did not say, “Where are God’s prophetic declarations?” “You promised me kingship, yet I am forced to serve; you offered authority as a gift, yet I do not even enjoy the freedom common to everyone. I descended from freedom into servitude; I went from ease into prison.” He entertained no such thought, but persevered and waited for events to reach a blessed conclusion. And who will testify that he looked forward to a blessed outcome of events and did not waver? There were, it says, two servants of Pharaoh in prison. They had dreams and were sad. Joseph said to them, “Why are you sad?” And they said, “We have had dreams, and there is no one to interpret them.” He did not say, “Let no one pay attention to dreams; let my dreams serve as an example for other dreams.” To show that he was intent on his own dreams coming true, he said, “Tell me, and I will explain them to you.” Have your own dreams come true at all, that you should interpret those of others? He interpreted the dreams and looked forward to the fulfillment of his own dreams. Pay close attention; move from the foreshadowing to the truth. If you wish to learn about Joseph’s circumstances, do not learn from his brothers, for envy conceals the truth and casts the free man into servitude. [?] Do not learn from the Ishmaelites either, for they too bought the free man as a slave; nor from his mistress, for she slandered him because of her own shamelessness. But if you wish to understand what sort of person Joseph was, ask his father, and he will say, “A son, and a beloved son.” Come to Christ. If you wish to understand what sort of person Christ is, do not learn from the Jews, for envy conceals the truth; nor from the idolaters, for they hate the destroyer of their images; nor from the schismatics, for just as the Ishmaelites did not know that they had bought a free man, so the schismatics do not recognize him, and therefore make the free man a slave. Nor from the Jews, for they are enemies of the cross; nor from the idolaters, for they hate the one who exposes their idols; nor from the heretics, for they are a likeness of Ishmael, who was not born of the free woman but of the slave woman. The Ishmaelites are a foreshadowing of the schismatics, and the sons of the free woman a foreshadowing of believers. When the patriarch blessed Joseph, he said, “Your blessing is from the dew of heaven and from the richness of the earth.” Pay attention: those are God’s gifts, bestowed from heaven and earth. The gifts were not given to Ishmael, for he did not have this. “By the sword,” he says, “you shall live.” The Ishmaelites have no other occupation by which they can gain any profit except the sword alone. The schismatics resemble them: they believe neither the declarations from heaven nor the prophets, but oppose them with the sword. And rightly so, for they are Ishmaelites, since they do not live by the word of God but by the sword of folly.

From now on, do not learn what Christ is like from Jews, idolaters, or heretics. Rather, if you wish to understand, learn his nature from his own root. See what his Father testifies about him: “This is my beloved Son; listen to him.” The Father calls him Son, and you call him a creature? “This,” he says, “is my beloved Son.” And again: “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son.” But does the Father not convince you? Do the words of the prophets not fill you with awe? Do the ranks of the apostles not command your respect? Let the demons put you to shame. For you do not heed the Father, who says, “This is my beloved Son,” nor Paul, who proclaims, “You are the Son of the living God,” nor Isaiah, who calls him mighty God. You have denied the Scriptures; at least show respect before the demons. Matthew says: “Demons came out of many people and cried out, ‘You are the Son of God.’” Likewise, Mark says that they agreed in their words and said: “We know who you are, Son of God.” Likewise, Luke declares that when the demons saw him, they fell down before him, cried out, and said, “We know who you are, Son of God. [?] before the time to judge us.” Demons confess him to be the Son of God, and you call him a creature? You are in great distress, for you make the demons appear more righteous than yourself. An abundance of evils makes those who are less wicked appear righteous. For this reason, because of Jerusalem’s abundance of evils, he also said to her, “Sodom was more righteous than you,” meaning that, compared with your sins, the city of the Sodomites appeared righteous.

You have an example; bow down to the truth. For if Joseph had not gone to Egypt, the land of the Egyptians would have died of famine. And if the Giver of life had not come into the world, the whole world would have died from hunger for the divine Word. And that God, the divine Word, is food—listen: “Behold, I will send you not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord.” O wonders! How the pattern was portrayed beforehand in the prophet! You have seen the pattern in Joseph; see also the pattern of the resurrection in Daniel. They cast Daniel into the pit, not by the will of Darius and Cyrus. Christ goes up onto the cross with Pilate’s reluctant consent. The united princes compelled King Darius, and the united Jews compelled Pilate. Darius went early to see the pit and Daniel, to see whether he was alive. The apostles and the women went early to the tomb to see whether the Living One was alive.

Turn, heretics, from unbelief to faith. Do not be worse than water. Water saw Jesus and became wine; yet you say “Son” and call him a servant. He performed his first sign in Cana of Galilee, so that the saying might be fulfilled: “Galilee of the Gentiles—the people who sat in darkness saw a great light.” The first sign took place at a wedding, because the first increase of the human race comes from marriage, and a wedding is the root of the human plant. He blesses the root so that he may bless the branches. And I marvel at this: not merely that he was invited and agreed to go, but that he did not go to some distinguished house where a wedding was taking place, but to a wedding in the house of a poor man. The man in whose house the wedding took place was poor—so poor that even the wine ran out. He was poor in possessions, but became rich in the treasures of truth.

The Lord appeared and changed the water into wine. His mother reminds him: “They have no wine,” she says—she who was his mother according to the flesh and his handmaid according to his divinity. She was a maidservant [?] according to his divine nature, and became a mother according to the divine dispensation. He was her God and her son: God according to his lordship, and son according to the dispensation. “They have no wine.” “What is there between me and you, woman? My hour has not yet come.” At this point some understood that he was promising something of a different kind. But he reproaches his mother because she still regarded the Lord of mankind as a man. He rebuked her, not because she reminded him, but because she reminded him as though he were a man. Many thought that “My hour has not yet come” meant “The time for miracles has not yet come.” But if it had not come, how could you perform the miracle? Rather, he reproaches his mother for reminding him needlessly and at the wrong time, and because God has no need to be reminded. “The time for my revelation has not yet come, for no one yet knows who I am.” And so that you may learn that he said those words not to [?] the miracle, but to call his power to mind, his mother, recognizing his dignity, says, “Whatever he tells you, do it.”

He spoke and changed the water into wine—he who turns water into oil. For through the olive tree he turns dew into oil, and through the grain plant into wheat, and through other plants into fragrant herbs, and through trees into fruit. In everything he gives all plants their individual flavors: there is one rain, but many different flavors are produced. Do not marvel at his changing water into wine, but marvel greatly that throughout all creation he turns the same rain into different colors and flavors, and blood into milk, and all these things too into their individual colors and flavors. They disregarded his great works because of their daily familiarity with them, while anything new in his sudden intervention seemed wonderful. Otherwise, why do you not marvel at how he turns blood in women’s breasts into the white substance of milk? Why are you not amazed that he changes dark hair into white, something that the skill of dyers cannot possibly dye? It is possible to dye something white black, but to make something black white is utterly impossible. It is not possible to dye blood, nor to turn something white once it has been dyed red. Yet he turns dark blood into white blood and changes black hair into white hair, so that you may learn that nature does not produce this on its own, but that he established a law for nature to be this way.

So when you see him going to a wedding and making water into wine, marvel; but know that these are only tastes of his great works. It is great, but not in relation to the worker of wonders; rather, we benefit from it through that love. And so it is right and fitting to understand that the miracles of the giver of life were very small in relation to him, but very great to those who benefited from them. Moses bears witness that this is so when he recounts to them the wonders performed in the land of the Egyptians: “Remember how the Lord your God brought you out of the land of the Egyptians with great signs and mighty deeds.” See how he marveled at the wonders. See also how the worker of miracles considers his deeds small: “I did all this to the Egyptians so that you might tell your children’s children what a game I played with the Egyptians.” Do you see? What seems miraculous to us is play to God. But enough of this for now.

May the light of Christ dawn upon us, and may the divine word enlighten our souls, so that we may strip off the works of darkness, and put on the works of light, make our preaching shine through our words, and adorn with deeds the promise we have made; so that through words, deeds, and faith, and by God's favor, we may send up glory to the most holy Trinity forever. Amen.
